newsitem.title: UK: UK's Ashdown, former soldier, fights for votes.
newsitem.headline: UK's Ashdown, former soldier, fights for votes.

text.p: Paddy Ashdown, a former marine commando, is fighting a losing battle trying to persuade Britons that a vote for his Liberal Democrat party will carry the same weight as one for Tony Blair's Labour party.

The craggily handsome leader of the third force in British politics is popular with voters and has campaigned tirelessly for Thursday's election, often inspiring something close to pop star hysteria among young and old voters.
But however popular he is, Ashdown's party only attracts around 15 percent support in opinion polls.
Thanks to a political culture that always threatens to bury third forces, the Liberal Democrats look unlikely to improve on the 26 seats they already hold in parliament.

Ashdown, however, believes his party's strength at local level will pay dividends on Thursday. Tactical voting by Britons determined to oust the Conservatives at any cost could also be to his advantage in areas of southern England.
By 1996, after 7-1/2 years under Ashdown, the Liberals were Britain's second party of local government, having overtaken the Conservatives in terms of council seats held.

They could also credibly claim to have influenced the Labour Party into adopting the most far-reaching plans for constitutional reform in its recent history, including parliaments for Scotland and Wales.
Things had moved a long way since July 1988 when the little-known Ashdown was elected leader of the Liberal Democrats -- a job he later described as the toughest thing he ever did.
Then, the party was losing members, reeling from a brief but damaging alliance with the even smaller Social Democrat Party, plagued by in-fighting and running a hefty deficit.
Ashdown said he had no natural gifts as a politician and had to work hard at tasks such as speech-writing.
But he gained in stature and credibility during the Gulf War in 1991 which gave him the chance to display a unique combination of military experience and political judgement.

Then, months before the 1992 general election, he was rocked by revelations of a brief relationship he had with his former secretary in 1988, a minor scandal which earned him the newspaper nickname Paddy Pantsdown. But the impact faded when his wife Jane, by whom he has had two children, stood by him.
At that election, the Liberals won 17.8 percent of the votes, but just 20 of the 651 seats in parliament thanks to Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system.

By-election successes and a defection by a disillusioned Conservative raised the figure to 26, with Ashdown adding to his reputation as a foreign affairs expert with trips to Bosnia at the height of the fighting there.

But the party's progress faltered when Tony Blair became Labour leader in 1994 and set about moving his party rapidly to the political centre ground the Liberals traditionally occupied. Labour now holds an opinion poll lead of about 20 points.

At a party conference in that year, Ashdown seemed to lose control of his party, which passed a motion sympathetic to the legalisation of soft drugs and became the first British party publicly to discuss an end to the monarchy.
A party song dating from that conference, beloved by fiercely-individualistic Liberals, contains the lines "Didn't we have a lovely time/Upsetting Paddy Ashdown".

Ashdown responded to the Blair threat by abandoning the Liberal claim to be "equidistant" between the Conservatives and Labour, making it clear that if Blair needed him to sustain him in government, he was ready to help.
Jeremy John Ashdown was born in India on February 27, 1941, the eldest son of an Indian army colonel. His father became a pig-farmer in Northern Ireland when Paddy was five years old.
Ashdown was educated at an English private school where he earned the nick-name Paddy because of his strong Irish accent.

On leaving school, he saw active service with Royal Marine commando units in the jungles of Borneo, and on the streets of Belfast. He later commanded a unit of the special boat service in the Far East and studied Mandarin in Hong Kong, becoming a first-class Chinese interpreter.
After leaving the marines, he joined Britain's mission to the United Nations in Geneva as a diplomat. In 1976 he abandoned that career and returned to England to join the Liberals.
